scope: Read-only exact retained evidence already visible to the terminal parent review; no retrieval, new scientific evidence or computation.

entries.text: Q1P15-b2-009 recovery update: searched '"energy gap" "fast" "correlation" "LH2" exponential fluctuations time amplitude' and '"Relation between Dephasing Time" supporting information'. Recovered primary author manuscript Olbrich et al., Theory and Simulation of the Environmental Effects on FMO Electronic Transitions, DOI https://doi.org/10.1021/jz2007676, via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3144632/?pdf=1 (HTTP 200, 178470 bytes; saved emmy/FMO-fast-primary.html/.txt, SHA256 in emmy/FMO-fast-provenance.json). Table 1 gives explicitly quantified two-exponential covariance Fit 2, including amplitudes in \(10^{-5}\) eV squared and fast times around 4 fs; unlike the 2016 dephasing paper's approximate drop, these are paired amplitudes and times. I am testing that primary Fit 2 under the existing constant-dipole cumulant, common carrier/damping/prefactor/instrument assumptions, with fixed-variance time swaps. This is a BChl cofactor model in FMO, not a Q ligand. Oscillatory intramolecular terms are omitted by Fit 2 and its 5 fs sampled trajectory does not resolve a 4 fs decay robustly enough to treat the fitted times as precision measurements.

Q1P15-b2-009 primary recovery: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3144632/?pdf=1 retrieved HTTP 200 to ada/FMO-primary.html/.txt, with checksum/status in ada/FMO-retrieval-provenance.json. Olbrich et al., Theory and Simulation of the Environmental Effects on FMO Electronic Transitions, DOI https://doi.org/10.1021/jz2007676, Table 1 gives two-exponential electronic-gap covariance fits for protein-bound BChls. The averaged BChl 1-6 row has fast covariance amplitude \(213.30\times10^{-5}\) eV squared and decay time \(4.04\) fs, slow amplitude \(43.47\times10^{-5}\) eV squared and time \(138.98\) fs (ada/FMO-primary.txt:378-439). Fast standard deviation is \(0.046185\) eV and \(\sigma_f\tau_f/\hbar\approx0.2835\), so a fast-modulation component is supported by a primary protein simulation. This is an effective fitted component with unresolved oscillations, not a Q ligand or direct experimental confirmation; the underlying sampling is 5 fs and Fit 1 includes 13 damped oscillations whereas Fit 2 omits them (:278,:345-369). I am computing the two-component prefactored control, without inventing a physical competing pose.

Q1P15-b2-009 executable two-component check: ada/fast_component_check.py and ada/fast_component_results.json use Table-1 BChl1-6 covariance amplitudes/times (ada/FMO-primary.txt:378-439), independent stationary Gaussian components, constant dipole, the common assumed 2.78 eV carrier/50 fs damping, photon-energy prefactor and assumed 1 nm Gaussian instrument FWHM at 446 nm. Component products are \(0.28347\) fast and \(4.40232\) slow. Dynamic FWHM is \(0.08014129\) eV versus matched-total-variance static \(0.13413430\) eV. Thus a physically simulated protein-pigment parameter set can depart markedly from the static limit; the PYP result in #72 must not be generalised to all protein chromophores. To test discriminatory rather than common line-narrowing information, a COUNTERFACTUAL swaps only the fast time \(4.04\to4.56\) fs (the latter is a reported BChl7 time) holding BOTH component variances and slow time fixed. Static spectra are then identical; dynamic width increases by \(0.00217644\) eV, approximately \(0.35\) of assumed instrument FWHM \(0.0062330\) eV. These are not two reported matched-variance bound ensembles. Assumed plus/minus 10 percent component-standard-deviation perturbations give width ranges \([0.0724072,0.0881923]\) and \([0.0742307,0.0907360]\) eV. Their overlap is a sensitivity caution, not a confidence interval or proof of nondetection, especially if model errors are correlated. Timestep halving changes baseline width by \(3.7\times10^{-12}\) eV. Fit2 omits strong oscillatory covariance and has a fast fitted time below the source 5 fs sampling interval; no uncertainty of that time fit is supplied. Source https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3144632/ supplies primary simulation evidence for fast components, not experimentally verified Q pose dynamics, a matched-variance physical discriminator or nuisance-calibrated advantage.

Q1P15-b2-009 quantified primary/control result: FMO Table-1 averaged BChl 1-6 Fit 2 (emmy/FMO-fast-primary.txt:101-151; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3144632/) has covariance amplitudes \(\eta_f=0.002133\), \(\eta_s=0.0004347\) eV squared and times \(4.04,138.98\) fs. Therefore component standard deviations are \(0.0461844,0.0208495\) eV and products \(\sqrt{\eta_i}\tau_i/\hbar=0.28347,4.40232\): a primary protein-simulation fit DOES support a fast-modulation component alongside a slow component. Executed emmy/fast_component_check.py with \(C(t)=\eta_f e^{-t/\tau_f}+\eta_s e^{-t/\tau_s}\), independent Gaussian components and additive cumulant; results emmy/fast_component_results.json. Kept the earlier imposed 2.78 eV carrier, constant dipole, 50 fs damping, photon-energy prefactor and Gaussian instrument FWHM 0.006233 eV (assumed 1 nm at 446 nm). These carrier/instrument assumptions are controls, not FMO or Q measurements. Dynamic versus matched-total-variance static FWHM is \(0.08014215\) versus \(0.13413518\) eV. Freezing only the fast covariance while retaining its variance gives \(0.13355623\) eV. Thus this source-scale mixed model permits substantial motional narrowing, unlike the PYP slow-bath example; it establishes a dynamical correction to a static line shape, not competing-pose discrimination. Counterfactual fast-time swaps 3.79 versus 4.56 fs (times in the same primary table, applied to identical component amplitudes/slow time) give widths \(0.07907120,0.08231874\) eV; static spectra coincide exactly. Their dynamical-only difference \(0.00324754\) eV is below the assumed instrument FWHM. Assumed simultaneous plus/minus 10 percent component-standard-deviation changes give base widths \([0.07240976,0.08819295]\) eV, a sensitivity span larger than that time-only difference. These are not source confidence limits or a calibrated detection threshold. Halving time step 0.2 to 0.1 fs changes base width by \(1.72\times10^{-7}\) eV. Fit 2 neglects oscillatory covariance, the underlying 5 fs sampling limits the fast-time fit, and model/background/population errors are uncalibrated. No same-Q-ligand pose difference or demonstrated bound-drug fast-modulation regime is established. Read Ada #74: independently recovered parameters/conventions and product agree; our source is a protein-bound cofactor, not a verified Q chromophore.

Cross-check of Emmy #76 and closure of Q1P15-b2-008/-009: independent retrieval agrees on primary FMO Fit2 amplitudes/times and component bath products. My Simpson two-component propagation gives dynamic/static widths \(0.08014129/0.13413430\) eV, agreeing with her trapezoidal control to about \(9\times10^{-7}\) eV; the different time-swap endpoints explain our different counterfactual increments. ada/fast_component_grid_check.json refines energy spacing from \(0.00025\) to \(0.000125\) eV with six-standard-deviation Gaussian support: baseline changes \(5.6\times10^{-7}\) eV and the \(4.04\to4.56\) fs increment changes \(1.6\times10^{-7}\) eV. These numerical checks establish the simplified classical model calculation, not the covariance fit or Q suitability. Established this call: #72 demotes the dynamical-only width argument for the recovered PYP values, where static supplies almost all contrast; #74-75 recover a primary simulated fast component in a protein-bound cofactor and show mixed-regime motional narrowing plus a matched-variance counterfactual temporal increment. This keeps temporal information as a conditional extension, not the default presumed pose discriminator. Neither control is an observed or predicted Q pose difference. Missing remain verified bright transitions/window/background, original-anchor coordinates/maps, actual competing-pose gap/dipole trajectories and populations, covariance-fit uncertainty/oscillatory structure, electronic-model discrepancy and calibrated experimental fractions/noise/resolution. Instrument FWHM and assumed model perturbations are not detection thresholds. No classically infeasible electronic model, quantum-resource advantage, realised molecular discrimination or novelty determination has been established. I have read through #76, agree with its qualified conclusion, and supply no scientific verdict.

Cross-check of Ada #72/#74/#75: independently recovered primary covariance conventions agree with #71/#73/#76. Inspected ada/fast_component_check.py:8-34: its 0.00025 eV grid, Simpson time quadrature and 700 fs cutoff differ from my 0.0005 eV grid, trapezoidal quadrature and 500 fs cutoff. Its baseline dynamic/static widths and my #76 agree within \(9\times10^{-7}\) eV; its 4.04-to-4.56 fs time-only increment \(0.00217644\) eV agrees with subtraction of my corresponding widths within \(2\times10^{-7}\) eV. The distinct \(0.00324754\) eV in #76 compares 3.79-to-4.56 fs, so it is not a conflicting result. Ada's base/time-swap assumed amplitude-sensitivity ranges overlap, but correlated model error could cancel in a difference; neither our absolute-width span nor overlap proves nondetection. The important distinction is common motional narrowing versus discriminatory temporal contrast: the primary FMO fit supplies the former, while only counterfactual matched-variance time swaps supply the latter here. This reopens a conditional mixed fast/slow regime without undoing the PYP-specific demotion in #71/#72.

Executable extension of #75/#77 and Emmy #86: ada/fast_damping_nuisance.txt derives the fast Gaussian asymptote, in which the effective decay is \(\gamma+\eta_f\tau_f/\hbar^2\) plus a multiplicative amplitude. ada/fast_damping_nuisance_check.py:36-55, output ada/fast_damping_nuisance_results.json, keeps the same assumed carrier/prefactor/instrument and the primary FMO Fit2 variances (ada/FMO-primary.txt:378-439; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3144632/). To mimic the counterfactual 4.04-to-4.56 fs time change using the ORIGINAL fast time, increase extra damping by \(0.00256013\) inverse fs: the imposed 50 fs damping becomes 44.32598 fs, equivalent extra energy HWHM 0.00168511 eV. Fitting a free intensity scale gives 1.013064. The remaining full-spectrum Euclidean residual is 0.35557 times the raw time-contrast norm, and 0.006664 times the target-spectrum norm. These are arbitrary unweighted channel norms, not noise-calibrated information, thresholds or detection results; this explicit feasible nuisance construction is not an optimised profile. It absorbs much but not all of the waveform contrast, with early-time transients retaining a residual. Independent damping/intensity calibration could constrain this direction. Emmy #86 uses the reverse compensation, lengthening damping for the altered-time model to recover the original asymptote; its different damping value is therefore consistent, not a numerical disagreement. Common motional narrowing and a fast fitted component still do not establish pose information.

branches/branch-2/ada/fast_component_res.assumptions: Independent stationary Gaussian components, constant dipole, common assumed 2.78 eV carrier, 50 fs extra damping, photon-energy prefactor, assumed Gaussian 1 nm FWHM at 446 nm; oscillations omitted.
branches/branch-2/ada/fast_component_res.limitations: Fast fitted time below 5 fs MD snapshot interval; no source confidence interval; time swap is not a reported matched-variance physical pair; instrument and model spread are assumed; no Q or experimental discrimination.

branches/branch-2/ada/fast_damping_nuisa.assumptions: Same control carrier, variances, slow time, Gaussian covariance, energy prefactor and instrument as ada/fast_component_check.py; arbitrary unweighted energy-channel norm; positive adjustable damping and free multiplicative amplitude.
branches/branch-2/ada/fast_damping_nuisa.limitations: Explicit nuisance construction, not an optimised profile, calibrated noise norm, detection threshold, fitted physical lifetime, or a Q pose spectrum. Early-time covariance leaves nonzero residual. Instrument, damping and time swap are assumptions.

branches/branch-2/emmy/fast_component_re.assumptions: Independent Gaussian components, constant dipole, common imposed 2.78 eV carrier and 50 fs damping; photon-energy prefactor; Gaussian 1 nm FWHM at 446 nm locally converted to energy; no excitonic coupling, oscillatory covariance, thermal correction or population nuisance. Time swaps are counterfactual, not observed FMO cases or Q poses.
